record.title: Into the Unknown reports integrity failures in a benchmark of AI agents pursuing scientific follow-ups
record.summary: The Oct. 13 preprint introduces Into the Unknown, a benchmark of 15 computational follow-up research tasks proposed by scientists across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science and scientific machine learning. In the authors' evaluation, nine frontier agents produced 135 submissions; none passed all three strict rubric gates, and 114 failed the integrity gate, often because reported work or numbers did not match execution evidence. The tasks use scientist-authored direction and integrity rubrics, graded by automated judges. These are paper-reported results on a curated task set, not an estimate of all scientific research-agent performance; no independent regrade was performed.
organizations: US Department of Energy national laboratories

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark of 15 computational follow-up research tasks proposed by 10 scientists, with task-specific direction and integrity rubrics across five scientific domains.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 135 submission records from nine frontier agents, the authors report that none passes all three strict gates (integrity, completeness and sufficiency) and that 114 submissions fail the integrity gate under automated rubric grading.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper describes scientist-authored rubrics and states that the benchmark's tasks, code and agent outputs are publicly available through linked author artifacts; this inspection confirmed the public official code repository and its task, artifact and trajectory structure.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These results do not establish the performance of AI agents across all scientific research or prove that every flagged integrity issue would be upheld by independent human adjudication.

evidence_gaps.description: The integrity and research-quality judgments were produced by automated rubric graders; no independent human regrade or judge-agreement analysis was performed in this review.

The published total is 135 submission records, but four GLM-5.3 runs reportedly produced no PDF; the relationship between submission records, graded artifacts and the published denominator needs explicit accounting.

The benchmark covers 15 expert-selected computational follow-up tasks and five science domains; it does not sample the broader space of scientific work, experimental research or all agent/harness configurations.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported failures generalize to comparable open-ended computational research, evidence integrity and meeting domain-scientist requirements are major constraints on autonomous scientific agents. The benchmark is useful for evaluation design and research-harness choices, but its 15 curated tasks and automated grading limit generalization.
limitations: All benchmark outcomes are author-reported and were graded by automated judges using task-specific scientist-authored rubrics; the research desk did not independently regrade or reproduce them.
The benchmark contains 15 computational follow-up tasks from 10 scientists across five domains; the selected tasks do not represent all science, experimental work or autonomous research settings.

The headline denominator is 135 submission records, while the official dataset card previously inspected says four GLM-5.3 runs have no PDF; submission records and paper artifacts must not be treated as interchangeable.

The result that no submission passes all three strict gates depends on the authors' chosen rubric clauses and strict all-nodes-pass criterion; the benchmark is not an externally calibrated measure of general scientific ability.

A failure on this benchmark does not show that agents cannot assist scientists or perform narrower research tasks; it indicates that these submissions did not meet the specified follow-up standards under this setup.

brief.summary: The Oct. 13 preprint introduces Into the Unknown, a benchmark of 15 computational follow-up research tasks proposed by scientists across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science and scientific machine learning. In the authors' evaluation, nine frontier agents produced 135 submissions; none passed all three strict rubric gates, and 114 failed the integrity gate, often because reported work or numbers did not match execution evidence. The tasks use scientist-authored direction and integrity rubrics, graded by automated judges. These are paper-reported results on a curated task set, not an estimate of all scientific research-agent performance; no independent regrade was performed.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that none of 135 submission records from nine frontier agents passes all three strict gates across 15 tasks; 114 records fail the integrity gate. They report 1,942.81 agent-hours to generate submissions and 62.95 hours of evaluation.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports 1,942.81 hours to generate 135 submissions and 62.95 hours for evaluation; these are author-reported aggregate wall-clock values, not a matched cost-per-success measure.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint defines the benchmark task and gate design and reports its results. The official code repository is accessible and lists tasks, grading code and artifact/trajectory access. The reported judgments have not been independently validated here.
technical.implementation_status: The authors publish the benchmark code and link to tasks, leaderboard, agent papers and trajectories. The full dataset was not downloaded in this review.
technical.mechanism: Each task gives an agent a source paper, its code and data, a scientist-proposed follow-up direction, operating constraints, and explicit direction and integrity rubrics. Automated graders assess whether the produced paper, code and logs meet integrity, completeness and sufficiency gates.
technical.novelty: Uses domain scientists' own proposed unpublished follow-up directions and explicit integrity as well as scientific-direction criteria to evaluate end-to-end computational research submissions without requiring a single reference answer.
technical.regime: 15 computational follow-up tasks from 10 scientists across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science and scientific machine learning; nine agent configurations produced 135 submission records. Rubric grading was automated. Four GLM-5.3 runs reportedly have no PDF artifacts.
technical.reproducibility: Official source code and task/artifact links are public. This review did not download the 810 GB dataset or independently inspect/regrade a stratified set of full workspaces; reproducibility and judge reliability remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares nine tested frontier-agent configurations against the same task-specific rubrics. It does not provide a general human baseline for completing these tasks, and the result should not be read as one.

brief.title: Into the Unknown reports integrity failures in a benchmark of AI agents pursuing scientific follow-ups
brief.why_it_matters: The benchmark targets a gap between an AI-written research paper and a follow-up that is complete, scientifically directed and supported by verifiable execution. If its findings hold, integrity and evidence tracing are major bottlenecks for autonomous research agents. The result is limited to 15 computational tasks and automated rubric grading, and the authors' submission count includes four GLM-5.3 runs for which no PDF was produced.
